# The user story before the token story

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Write what the protocol does for a user in one sentence with no token in it; if you cannot, you have an instrument, not a product. Then give each audience one belief and one piece of evidence, and keep a claims register with no yield numbers, no 'safe' and every audit named and dated. MiCA and the SEC's 2026 interpretation both make public claims part of the legal record.

Write what the protocol does for a user in one sentence with no token in it. If you cannot, you have an instrument, not a product. Then give each audience one belief and one piece of evidence, and keep a claims register that survives both an audit and a narrative rotation: no yield numbers, no "safe", every audit named and dated. Regulators now read the same claims: MiCA requires marketing to be fair, clear, not misleading and consistent with the white paper, and the SEC's 2026 interpretation turns on what a team promised in public.

*This is not legal advice. Claims rules are jurisdiction-specific; get your own counsel.*

## The token collapses your audiences

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) set the rule: one product truth, a belief per audience. Crypto makes that harder because the token merges the audiences into a single word.

A holder may be an investor, a community member and a customer at the same time. Each wants something different. The investor wants a business. The customer wants a thing that works. The community member wants a reason to stay.

When the deck leads with the token, each reader filters it through their own need, and none of them is satisfied. The token story drowns the product story because it is louder and easier to write. So the order matters. Product truth first. Token second. Always. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers the general method; this is the crypto edition.

## One sentence, no token

Write what the protocol does for a user. One sentence. The token is not allowed in it.

The shape is simple: this lets a certain kind of user do a certain thing, without a certain cost or dependency. If you cannot write it, you do not have a product yet. You have an instrument. Some projects are instruments, and that is fine, but say so and position accordingly.

Test the sentence on someone who has never read your docs. If their first question is "and what is the token for", good. That is the second sentence, not the first.

The sentence also does legal work. The SEC and CFTC interpretation of March 2026 treats a token whose value depends on a network's programmatic functioning differently from one sold with promises of an issuer's managerial efforts, and Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous". A team whose first sentence is about price is making a promise about price. A team whose first sentence is about a user is describing a product.

## A belief per audience

Each audience needs one belief and one piece of evidence.

| Audience | What they need to believe | What proves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Users | It works and I can exit | Live app, withdrawals working in normal and stressed weeks, a status page that tells the truth |
| Integrators and allocators | Safe to build on or deploy into | Current docs, named and dated audits, incident history, a plain risk page |
| Holders | The token has a job | A written description of what the token does in the system, and what it does not |
| Investors | There is a business under the token | Fees retained, costs, who pays and why |

Notice the holder row. "The token has a job" is a product claim, not a price claim. If the only job is "goes up", you do not have a belief. You have a hope. Our piece on [token or no token](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) covers what to do about that, and [protocol revenue](https://lowob.com/research/protocol-revenue-fees-real-yield-and-what-to-report/) covers the investor row's numbers.

The integrator row carries the heaviest evidence burden, because the downside is concrete. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025. An allocator reading "audited by leading firms" with no names, scopes or dates has learned nothing, and will assume the worst.

## The claims register, crypto edition

One truth, three audiences introduced the claims register: every public claim, its evidence, its owner, its date. Crypto adds hard lines.

| Rule | Why | Where regulators already draw the line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No yield numbers in marketing: not "up to", not "historical", not a screenshot | Yields change daily and read as a promise | MiCA Article 6 bars white-paper assertions on future value and requires a statement that the token may lose value in part or in full |
| No "safe", "secure", "risk-free" or "guaranteed" | If legal would not sign the word, it is a liability | MiCA Article 7 and the UK FCA both require promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading |
| Audits named: firm, scope, date, link; unaudited components listed | "Audited by leading firms" is a claim with no evidence | Allocators' diligence asks for exactly this |
| Deprecated docs removed, not banner-archived | Stale docs are how an integrator deploys against a contract you retired | MiCA Article 7 requires marketing consistent with the white paper; old docs are public claims too |
| Every number has an owner and a date | If nobody owns it, nobody corrects it | The SEC's 2026 interpretation weighs who said what, when and in which medium |

If nobody owns a claim, it comes down. In the UK, crypto promotions to consumers have been regulated since 8 October 2023 and must carry specific risk warnings; a promotion made outside the permitted routes can be a criminal offence. In the EU, MiCA Article 7 also requires marketing to be clearly identifiable as such and bars it before a required white paper is published.

> If legal would not sign the word, do not post it.

## Vocabulary and chain choice

Docs, app and deck must use the same names for the same things. "Vault" in the docs, "pool" in the app and "strategy" in the deck reads as three products. An allocator will assume you have three teams who do not talk.

Keep a glossary. One owner. When a name changes, it changes everywhere in the same week.

Chain choice is also a positioning statement, whether you intended it or not. Where you deploy picks your users, your integrators, your liquidity sources and your grant counterparties. Say why in one line. "We are here because our users are here" is positioning. "We are multi-chain" with no primary home is the absence of positioning. In the EU, the choice of venue and custody partner now also carries a regulatory test: since MiCA's transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, ESMA expects unauthorised service providers to stop onboarding and marketing to EU clients.

## The narrative trap

Labels rotate: RWA, AI, restaking and whatever is next. A label gets you attention this quarter and makes you a casualty of the rotation the quarter after.

The product truth must not contain the label. Use the label as a door people walk through, not as the foundation they stand on. If the only reason someone would use the protocol is the category it sits in, the protocol is the category's hostage.

Test it the same way as the token. Remove the label from the homepage. Check whether the first sentence still describes something a user wants. Our piece on [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/) covers the evidence that survives a rotation: named users, dated outcomes, numbers with owners.

Gateway card

### Before the next deck, page or post goes out

- One sentence describing what the protocol does for a user, with no token in it
- One belief and one piece of evidence each for users, integrators and allocators, holders and investors
- Claims register live: no yields, no "safe", every audit named, scoped and dated
- Deprecated docs removed, not banner-archived
- One glossary; docs, app and deck use identical names
- One line explaining the chain choice, and a homepage that still makes sense without this quarter's label

## lowob takeaways

- **Product first, token second.** The token merges your audiences; the user sentence separates them again.
- **One belief per audience.** Each with one piece of evidence that a sceptic can check.
- **Hard lines in the register.** No yields, no "safe", audits named and dated, every number owned.
- **Claims are legal facts.** In the EU and US, what you say in public shapes how the token is treated.
